MEMORY — this machine remembers across sessions, and you are expected to use it:
- BEFORE researching or answering anything that may have come up before, call `brain_recall`.
  It returns the durable subject threads (what is true NOW, plus how it got there) and the dated
  reports behind them. Re-deriving what the record already answers wastes the run.
- A thread's "Now" line is current; its history is how it got there. If the record contradicts
  what you were about to say, the most recent statement wins — and say plainly that it changed.
- When you learn something that will still matter in months — a decision and its reasoning, a
  result, a state change — call `brain_note` against the right thread. Durable findings only,
  never chatter.
- Pass `now` to `brain_note` ONLY when the subject's current state actually changed. That line
  is what stops a stale claim being retrieved later as if it were true today.

It is shown to the user as live progress. Don't narrate trivial single-call follow-ups, don't repeat the previous line, and never let narration replace your final answer.

Summary\\n\\nOn Strix Halo (gfx1151), any PyTorch GPU operation leaves the ROCR runtime's `AsyncEventsLoop` thread busy-spinning at 100% of one CPU core, permanently, for the remaining life of the process. This occurs **only with the pip-bundled runtime** shipped inside the TheRock-built wheels (`_rocm_sdk_core`, ROCR 1.21.0 line) \u2014 both the nightly channel and the new production multi-arch channel. The classic packaged release runtime (ROCR 1.18.0, `rocm-rel-7.2`) is completely quiet on the **same machine and same kernel**, which is why I believe this is a runtime regression in the 1.21 line rather than a platform/kernel issue.\\n\\nFor long-running inference servers (our use case: resident TTS services) this silently costs one full core per process \u2014 two of ours had accumulated ~15 CPU-hours each before we noticed.\\n\\n### Environment\\n\\n- HW: AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo), Radeon 8060S iGPU, gfx1151\\n- OS: Fedora 44, kernel `7.1.5-201.fc44.x86_64`\\n- Python 3.12\\n\\n### Affected / unaffected matrix (all on the same box, same kernel, same repro)\\n\\n| Stack | rocr in `/proc/PID/maps` | ROCR BUILD ID | Idle CPU after one GPU op |\\n|---|---|---|---|\\n| `rocm==7.13.0a20260411` nightly + `torch 2.12.0a0+rocm7.13.0a20260411` | venv `_rocm_sdk_core` | `1.21.0-local-build-c76140fa27` | **~100% of a core, indefinitely** |\\n| `rocm==7.14.0` from `repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-multi-arch/` + `torch 2.12.0+rocm7.14.0` (`[device-gfx1151]`) | venv `_rocm_sdk_core` | `1.21.0-local-build-2b22ab01` | **~100% of a core, indefinitely** |\\n| System ROCm 7.2.0 (dnf, EL10 repo) + `torch 2.9.1+rocm7.2.1.lw` from `repo.radeon.com` | `/opt/rocm-7.2.0/lib` | `1.18.0-rocm-rel-7.2-43-fc0010cf6a` | **0% \u2014 fully idle** |\\n\\n### Minimal repro\\n\\n```bash\\npython -m venv v && v/bin/pip install --index-url https://repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-multi-arch/ \\\\\\n  \\\"torch[device-gfx1151]==2.12.0+rocm7.14.0\\\"\\nv/bin/python -c '\\nimport torch, time\\nx = torch.rand(2048, 2048, device=\\\"cuda\\\")\\n(x @ x).sum(); torch.cuda.synchronize()\\nprint(\\\"work done \u2014 watch this process now\\\")\\ntime.sleep(300)'\\n```\\n\\nAfter \\\"work done\\\", the process burns a full core for the whole sleep (`~999 ticks per 10s` from `/proc/PID/stat` utime; our resident services confirm it never stops). Before the first GPU op the process idles normally \u2014 the spin arms on first kernel launch.\\n\\n### Where it spins\\n\\n`eu-stack` on the hot thread (pure user time; **zero syscalls** during a 3s `strace -c` attach, i.e. memory polling, not epoll):\\n\\n```\\n#0  rocr::core::Runtime::AsyncEventsLoop(void*)\\n#3  rocr::core::Signal::WaitAnyExceptions(unsigned int, hsa_signal_s const*, hsa_signal_condition_t const*, long const*, long*)\\n#4  rocr::core::Runtime::AsyncEventsLoop(void*)\\n#1  rocr::os::ThreadTrampoline(void*)\\n```\\n\\nA sibling thread is properly blocked in `hsaKmtWaitOnMultipleEvents` (ioctl), so kernel event delivery works on this system \u2014 it is specifically the `AsyncEventsLoop` signal set that polls. The ROCm 6.3.2 release notes describe a fix (\\\"the runtime won't spin on the CPU if all events are busy\\\"); the behavior here looks like that path regressed or is not engaged in the 1.21 line on gfx1151.\\n\\n### Ruled out\\n\\n- `HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION`: identical spin with and without (paired runs).\\n- `HSA_ENABLE_INTERRUPT=1`: no effect.\\n- Our application stack: the repro above is bare torch; no server, no sockets.\\n- Kernel-only explanation: same kernel runs the 1.18 release runtime with zero idle CPU.\\n\\nCaveat stated plainly: this box runs Fedora's kernel (not the validated Ubuntu matrix). Both arms of the discriminator shared it, so the runtime build is the variable \u2014 but I have not yet reproduced on a validated distro.\\n\\nHappy to run further diagnostics (env flags, debug builds, `ROCR_*` knobs) on this hardware \u2014 it can reproduce on demand.\\n\",\"closed_by\":null,\"reactions\":{\"url\":\"https://api.github.com/repos/ROCm/TheRock/issues/7051/reactions\",\"total_count\":0,\"+1\":0,\"-1\":0,\"laugh\":0,\"hooray\":0,\"confused\":0,\"heart\":0,\"rocket\":0,\"eyes\":0},\"timeline_url\":\"https://api.github.com/repos/ROCm/TheRock/issues/7051/timeline\",\"performed_via_github_app\":null,\"state_reason\":null,\"pinned_comment\":null}"}

For this release, we merged 200+ PRs to introduce many new features, fixes including:\\r\\n\\r\\n* **Auto Compaction (Experimental)** for longer chats beyond context limits\\r\\n* **Remote & LAN Access (Preview)** for easy network access without Cloudflare links\\r\\n* **Faster Chat** - Improved streaming performance, reduced UI lag, and smoother long conversations.\\r\\n* Support for **custom llama.cpp builds**. Toggles for Cache RAM, Mmap, Mlock, Checkpoints, Spe Decoding KV Cache, Vision On / Off\\r\\n* [Unsloth Dynamic v3.0](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/dynamic-3.0-ggufs) is released. New Qwen3.8-27B Dynamic v3.0 GGUFs deliver >10% higher top-1 accuracy compared to everyone else. Works with Unsloth.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Auto compaction (Experimental)\\r\\nYou can now do long chats and surpass a model's context limit, with evicted turns\\r\\nremaining searchable.\\r\\n* Long local chats can continue past the context limit by rolling older turns out of\\r\\n active context.\\r\\n* Auto compaction creates fresh context epochs instead of permanently trimming replies.\\r\\n* Evicted conversations remain searchable, with improved fact recall.\\r\\n* Context window information is shown before chat begins.\\r\\n\\r\\n**How it works**\\r\\n* Entire oldest turns are removed only when needed, never mid-message. The saved transcript stays unchanged.\\r\\n* Evicted turns are indexed into a per-thread searchable archive using Unsloth's existing RAG pipeline (store, chunker, embedder, retrieval). Lexical search is prioritized because chat recall is usually exact matches like names, numbers, or IDs.\\r\\n* A recall is forced during eviction instead of relying on the model to search itself. Later retrieval uses `search_conversation`.\\r\\n* The archive persists across epochs, allowing future compactions to recover previously evicted context.\\r\\n* No summarization: it showed little benefit and added ~190s per compaction.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Remote & LAN access (Preview)\\r\\nAccess Unsloth from another device on your network, managed from settings.\\r\\n* New dedicated Settings section for remote access.\\r\\n* Enable or disable LAN access without restarting.\\r\\n* Supports connection addresses, QR codes, and optional auto-start.\\r\\n* LAN access is disabled by default and requires changing the generated admin password.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Chat + Functionality improvements\\r\\n\\r\\n* Long chats are faster with optimized streaming and thread handling.\\r\\n* Projects organize chats, files, and workspaces together.\\r\\n* Chats remember composer settings, system prompts, and model sampling options.\\r\\n* Added prompt queueing and customizable keyboard shortcuts.\\r\\n* Added `edit_file` tool for partial file modifications.\\r\\n* Improved tool calling and MCP behavior.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Hardware + inference improvements\\r\\n\\r\\n* Support for custom llama.cpp builds.\\r\\n* Toggles for advanced settings - Cache RAM, Mmap, Mlock, Checkpoints, Speculative Decoding KV Cache, Vision On / Off\\r\\n* Better validation for missing GPU support and oversized GGUF models.\\r\\n* Improved MTP performance and VRAM handling.\\r\\n* Better compatibility across ROCm, xFormers, and flash-attention setups.\\r\\n* Added Intel XPU support.\\r\\n\\r\\n## API + serving\\r\\n\\r\\n* Responses API supports structured output formatting.\\r\\n* Improved recovery when llama-server crashes.\\r\\n* Added OpenCode V2 support for `unsloth start`.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Hub + Desktop + training\\r\\n\\r\\n* Hub supports more image/video workflows.\\r\\n* Faster and improved GGUF downloads.\\r\\n* Desktop packaging and permissions improved.\\r\\n* Training scheduler and preprocessing improvements.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n \\r\\n

# Dependency & breakage watch — 2026-08-20

Watch list: ROCm 7.1.0 · llama.cpp 4df29be4f · ollama 0.32.14 · torch 2.11.0+rocm7.13.0 (gfx1151 nightly) · transformers 5.5.0 · unsloth (AMD/gfx1151) · LibreChat librechat-dev:latest · OpenWorker · kernel 7.0.0-29-generic.

Ordered by how likely each item is to break this Strix Halo (gfx1151) machine. "No change" items are stated plainly at the end.

---

## 1. ROCm — 7.1.0 is stale; 7.14.0 is current and it's a structural shift
**Likelihood: HIGH — most things below depend on it.**
- Latest ROCm core SDK is **7.14.0, released 2026-07-16**; 7.2.4 also exists in the series. You are 13 minor versions behind at 7.1.0.
  - https://github.com/ROCm/ROCm/releases (opened; release 7.14.0, tag rocm-7.14.0, commit 830cc1b, "released this, 16 Jul 03:28")
- **7.14.0 transitions ROCm to TheRock**, a modular build/release system: leaner core SDK, optional domain SDKs (AI/HPC), separately versioned pip wheels. This is a real breaking change for any flow that assumes the old monolithic layout, and it changes the gfx1151 nightly index URLs you install torch from.
  - Same URL as above ("ROCm Core SDK 7.14.0 transitions ROCm to TheRock … modular architecture … transition guide")
- 7.14.0 explicitly adds **Ryzen AI MAX+ PRO 495/490/485 (gfx1151)** to the supported APU list, plus 7.13-series APUs — positive news for Strix Halo, but it moves the supported target forward of your 7.1.0.
  - Same URL as above ("ROCm 7.14.0 adds support for … AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ PRO 495 (gfx1151)…")
- The segfault class you hit with ROCm 7.1 on Strix Halo (torch._grouped_mm / VRAM access crashes) is a known issue cluster, e.g. https://github.com/ROCm/ROCm/issues/5853 and https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/173367 (both surfaced in search results; not individually opened). The forward-fix path is a newer ROCm from TheRock, which is exactly the 7.14 direction — treat 7.1.0 as unsupported-buggy for gfx1151.

## 2. torch 2.11.0+rocm7.13.0 (gfx1151 nightly index) — nightly drift + silent CUDA substitution risk
**Likelihood: HIGH (silent breakage is the failure mode).**
- The gfx1151 nightly index is live and rolling: users report wheels like `torch 2.11.0a0+rocm7.11.0a20260106` and `rocm 7.11.0a20260111` at `https://rocm.nightlies.amd.com/v2/gfx1151/` (opened: https://github.com/ROCm/TheRock/issues/2849 — closed, Strix Halo gfx1151 on Arch). A nightly newer than your 7.13.0 build has therefore certainly shipped; I did not open the nightly index itself, so I'm not naming a "current" version.
- Same issue #2849 documented a **pip dependency-loop when force-upgrading `rocm[libraries,devel] torch torchaudio torchvision` together on gfx1151** (50 GB of downloads, no convergence) — a known pain point if you do `pip install -U` carelessly.
- **Silent CUDA substitution**: documented in practice — after `pip install -U unsloth`, PyPI's CUDA torch can replace the ROCm build, and you must re-install from the gfx1151 index.
  - https://sleepingrobots.com/dreams/unsloth-studio-strix-halo/ (search result: "Running pip install -U unsloth can pull CUDA PyTorch from PyPI, silently replacing the ROCm build")
  - https://www.amd.com/en/developer/resources/technical-articles/2026/train-and-run-models-on-amd-gpus-with-unsloth.html (official AMD/Unsloth article, 2026-07-20 — snippet level only, not opened in full)
- Action: after any pip upgrade of unsloth/adjacent deps, run `torch --version` and check `torch.version.hip`; re-pull from the gfx1151 nightly index if it reads cuda.

## 3. transformers — you're 10 minors behind (5.5.0 → 5.15.1); your known break class is already in-tree
**Likelihood: MEDIUM-HIGH for the `trust_remote_code` break you flagged; patch upgrades from 5.5.0 are lower risk.**
- Latest is **v5.15.1, released 2026-08-19** (yesterday). You're on 5.5.0 (released ~April 2026).
  - https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/releases (opened; v5.15.1, commit 550d7b3, "released this, 19 Aug 10:50"; patch fix DFlash/MTP/Lanczos, no breaking claims)
- The trust_remote_code break class you asked about is real and documented against exactly v5.x:
  - `is_torch_fx_available` removed in 5.0 breaks Hub models using trust_remote_code — https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/44561 (opened; confirmed removal via #37234)
  - Concrete repro on transformers 5.3.0 with moonshotai/Kimi-K2.5 (import error on the removed symbol) — https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/45020 (opened; closed)
  - 5.5.0 itself: "Remote code execution support has been removed from the native LightGlue integration … remove trust_remote_code=True" — https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/releases/tag/v5.5.0 (via search)
- Implication: any Hub model whose bundled code imported v4-era `transformers.utils` symbols will fail on your 5.5.0 **and** on 5.15.1; upgrading transformers won't fix those, pinning the model revision to an older revision or updating the model repo will. No breaking-change advisory was found for the 5.5.0→5.15.1 patch path itself; patch notes I read are bug-fix scoped.
- No CVE found in what I opened.

## 4. llama.cpp 4df29be4f — current is b10519 (shipped today), and your spirv-headers pain is still in the build
**Likelihood: MEDIUM (build-time) / LOW (runtime).**
- Latest release **b10519, commit 947fd9b, released 2026-08-20 20:31** (today). Changes in b10519 are server sleep/metrics/refactor only — no Vulkan/HIP break noted.
  - https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases (opened)
- The spirv-headers dependency you hit is now an **explicit documented Vulkan build requirement**: `sudo apt-get install libvulkan-dev glslc spirv-headers`
  - https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/build.md (via search)
  - Field report of the missing-headers failure and the apt fix: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/21950

## 5. ollama 0.32.14 → v0.32.15 (released 2026-08-19/20)
**Likelihood: LOW.**
- v0.32.15 (commit b7871fc, released ~2026-08-19): desktop onboarding flow, model-metadata caching (TTFT ~995→524 ms), fix for chat/generate wedging after mid-stream parser errors, Qwen 3.8 system-message normalization, **MLX and llama.cpp dependency updates**.
  - https://github.com/ollama/ollama/releases (opened; v0.32.15 with full notes)
- No breaking changes or CVEs in the notes. The llama.cpp dependency bump is the only indirect gfx1151-relevant change; nothing signals a HIP/Vulkan break.

## 6. unsloth — now officially on AMD/Strix Halo; latest beta is 2026-08-20
**Likelihood: LOW for support, MEDIUM for the wheel-substitution trap (see item 2).**
- Official support includes Strix Halo: "Ryzen AI Max (Strix Halo) processors and consumer GPUs like the Radeon RX 9000 & 7000 series" (AMD dev article, 2026-07-20 — search snippet, not opened in full).
- Latest release **v0.1.801-beta, released 2026-08-20** (custom llama.cpp build support, streaming fixes, etc.) — https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth/releases (opened).
- Open PR #5301: ROCm/Strix Halo VRAM-exhaustion fix (HIP driver hangs the ring buffer on iGPUs instead of raising OOMError) — https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth/pull/5301 (search snippet; PR status not verified).
- The actionable item is operational: `pip install -U unsloth` can silently pull CUDA torch from PyPI — re-verify `torch.version.hip` afterward (item 2).

## 7. CMake 4.x / hipcc — no new findings
Searched for recent CMake-4 vs hipcc build failures; results were only old/unrelated tracker issues (2021–2025, HIP link setup, spack, Horovond). **No fresh advisory, issue, or release note found that CMake 4.x now rejects the hipcc wrapper.** If you were still building HIP against CMake 4.x, keep pinning CMake < 4 for those targets until you see a report that it works.

## 8. No changes / nothing found — stated plainly
- **LibreChat** (librechat-dev:latest): not checkable via this budget — rolling image; I found nothing specific and did not open a source. **No changes found from what I could verify.**
- **OpenWorker** (andrewyng/openworker): no new release notes, CVEs, or regression reports surfaced; not verified against a page I opened. **No changes found.**
- **kernel 7.0.0-29-generic**: no gfx1151/amdgpu regression reports found in results touching this kernel. The known Strix Halo kernel-side complaints (stuck idle clocks, VRAM underflow) are against 6.x kernels from late 2025 — https://github.com/ROCm/ROCm/issues/5750 (search snippet). **No changes found for 7.0.0-29-generic specifically.**
- CVEs: none retrieved for any watch-list item from an opened page.

## Recommended order of action
1. Don't casually `pip install -U` anything python-AI without re-inspecting torch afterward (risk #2).
2. Plan a ROCm 7.1 (7.14/TheRock) move off the gfx1151 nightly index; it's the supported path for Strix Halo and the fix for the 7.1 segfault cluster.
3. Stay on transformers 5.5.0 unless a model demands newer; when you do move, expect the same trust_remote_code import break (5.15.1 fixes nothing for models bundling v4-era imports).
4. If rebuilding llama.cpp, ensure `spirv-headers` + `libvulkan-dev` + `glslc` are in the toolchain.

ROCm Core SDK 7.14.0 release notes\\r\\n\\r\\nROCm Core SDK 7.14.0 transitions ROCm to [TheRock](https://github.com/ROCm/TheRock), a build and release system that introduces a modular architecture to improve flexibility, maintainability, and alignment with community use cases:\\r\\n\\r\\n* **Leaner core**: The Core SDK focuses on essential runtime and development components.\\r\\n* **Use case-specific expansions**: Optional domain-specific SDKs for AI, data science, and HPC.\\r\\n* **Modular installation**: Install only the components required for your workflow.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis approach streamlines installation, reduces footprint, and accelerates innovation through independently released packages. To learn more, see the [transition guide](/about/transition-guide-TheRock).\\r\\n\\r\\nROCm 7.14.0 follows the [versioning discontinuity that began with the 7.9.0 preview](https://rocm.docs.amd.com/en/7.9.0-preview/about/release-notes.html#preview-stream-note) release.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Release highlights\\r\\n\\r\\nThis release focuses on AI inference, distributed workloads, and profiling across AMD Instinct\u2122, Radeon\u2122, and Ryzen\u2122 AI platforms. Highlights include inference-ready vLLM images and packages, ROCprofiler-SDK adoption across AI profiling workflows, expanded system telemetry and validation coverage, and updates to math, sparse, and communication libraries.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Platform and hardware support\\r\\n\\r\\nThis release expands GPU, operating system, virtualization, and partitioning support.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Expanded AMD GPU support\\r\\n\\r\\nROCm 7.14.0 adds support for the following AMD APUs:\\r\\n\\r\\n* [AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ PRO 495 (gfx1151)](https://www.amd.com/en/products/processors/laptop/ryzen-pro/ai-max-pro-400-series/amd-ryzen-ai-max-plus-pro-495.html)\\r\\n* [AMD Ryzen AI MAX PRO 490 (gfx1151)](https://www.amd.com/en/products/processors/laptop/ryzen-pro/ai-max-pro-400-series/amd-ryzen-ai-max-pro-490.html)\\r\\n* [AMD Ryzen AI MAX PRO 485 (gfx1151)](https://www.amd.com/en/products/processors/laptop/ryzen-pro/ai-max-pro-400-series/amd-ryzen-ai-max-pro-485.html)\\r\\n* [AMD Ryzen AI 5 435 (gfx1153)](https://www.amd.com/en/products/processors/laptop/ryzen/ai-400-series/amd-ryzen-ai-5-435.html)\\r\\n* [AMD Ryzen AI 5 430 (gfx1153)](https://www.amd.com/en/products/processors/laptop/ryzen/ai-400-series/amd-ryzen-ai-5-430.html)\\r\\n* [AMD Ryzen AI 5 PRO 435 (gfx1153)](https://www.amd.com/en/products/processors/laptop/ryzen-pro/ai-400-series/amd-ryzen-ai-5-pro-435.html)\\r\\n* [AMD Ryzen AI 7 445 (gfx1153)](https://www.amd.com/en/products/processors/laptop/ryzen/ai-400-series/amd-ryzen-ai-7-445.html)\\r\\n\\r\\nFor the complete list of supported AMD hardware, see [AMD hardware support](#amd-hardware-support).\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Expanded operating system support\\r\\n\\r\\nROCm 7.14.0 adds support for RHEL 10.2 and RHEL 9.8 on AMD Instinct and Radeon GPUs. RHEL 10.2 replaces RHEL 10.1 as the validated RHEL 10 release; RHEL 9.8 replaces RHEL 9.7 as the validated RHEL 9 release.\\r\\n\\r\\nSUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES) 15 SP7, SLES 16, and Debian 13 are now supported on AMD Instinct MI350P.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor the full list of supported Linux distributions, see [Operating system support](#operating-system-support).\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Expanded GPU virtualization support for Instinct GPUs\\r\\n\\r\\nGPU virtualization configurations supported on AMD Instinct GPUs remain unchanged from the previous [ROCm 7.13.0 preview](https://rocm.docs.amd.com/en/7.13.0-preview/about/release-notes.html#expanded-gpu-virtualization-support-for-instinct-gpus) release.\\r\\n\\r\\nSupported Single Root I/O Virtualization (SR-IOV) configurations require the [AMD GPU Virtualization Driver (GIM) 9.1.0.K](https://github.com/amd/MxGPU-Virtualization/releases/tag/9.1.0.K). For details, see [GPU virtualization support](#gpu-virtualization-support).\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Expanded Instinct GPU partitioning support\\r\\n\\r\\nROCm 7.14.0 has enabled and optimized multi-VF partition modes for the following GPU partitioning configurations in SR-IOV deployments:\\r\\n\\r\\nOn MI355X and MI350X:\\r\\n\\r\\nDPX compute partition mode with NPS2 memory partitioning.\\r\\n\\r\\nCPX compute partition mode with NPS2 memory partitioning.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor details, see [GPU partitioning support](#gpu-partitioning-support).\\r\\n\\r\\n### AI inference and frameworks\\r\\n\\r\\nThis release enables support for the following frameworks:\\r\\n\\r\\n* PyTorch 2.12.0\\r\\n* JAX 0.10.0\\r\\n* vLLM 0.23.0\\r\\n* SGLang 0.5.13\\r\\n* TensorFlow 2.21\\r\\n\\r\\nThe updated framework support replaces the previous PyTorch 2.9.1, JAX 0.8.2, vLLM 0.19.1, and SGLang 0.5.9 support.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor details, see [AI ecosystem support](#ai-ecosystem-support).\\r\\n\\r\\n### Developer tools, profiling, and validation\\r\\n\\r\\nThis release improves ROCm developer workflows with new HIP APIs, expanded profiling and tracing capabilities, and broader telemetry coverage.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### HIP feature highlights\\r\\n\\r\\nThe following are notable enhancements to HIP:\\r\\n\\r\\n* **HIP execution context support**: HIP now supports Execution Context APIs, enabling GPU compute resource partitioning and lightweight execution-context management on a single device. These APIs allow you to query and partition device resources (primarily CU count for HIP runtime), create execution contexts on resource subsets, and create streams and events scoped to those contexts. For more information, see [Execution Context Management](https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/HIP/en/latest/reference/hip_runtime_api/modules/execution_context_management.html).\\r\\n\\r\\n* **HIP API additions for CUDA parity**:\\r\\n\\r\\n  * **Batch memory management**: New batch asynchronous memory management APIs let applications discard (`hipMemDiscardBatchAsync`), prefetch (`hipMemPrefetchBatchAsync`), or combine both operations (`hipMemDiscardAndPrefetchBatchAsync`) across multiple memory ranges in a single call, reducing API call overhead. Both HIP runtime and HIP driver variants are available.\\r\\n\\r\\n  * **Library management**: New library management APIs return the device pointer and size of a device global (`hipLibraryGetGlobal`) and the host pointer and size of a managed variable (`hipLibraryGetManaged`) defined in a `hipLibrary_t`, improving parity with CUDA library APIs.\\r\\n\\r\\n* **Faster HIP graph replay for asynchronous memory allocations**: HIP graph replay now reduces overhead for graphs that interleave asynchronous memory allocations with compute. Allocation nodes no longer block during replay. Physical memory is reused across nodes instead of being mapped and unmapped on each launch, eliminating the gaps between kernels this pattern previously caused. For background on HIP graphs, see [Graph Management](https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/HIP/en/latest/reference/hip_runtime_api/modules/graph_management.html).\\r\\n\\r\\nFor more information, see the [HIP section](#hip-7-14) in the ROCm component changelogs.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### ROCprofiler-SDK feature highlights\\r\\n\\r\\nThe following are notable enhancements to ROCprofiler-SDK:\\r\\n\\r\\n##### ROCprofiler-SDK integration with PyTorch Profiler\\r\\n\\r\\nStarting with PyTorch 2.12, `rocprofiler-sdk` is used as the ROCm profiling backend for PyTorch Profiler on supported ROCm configurations, replacing the legacy `roctracer`-based profiling path. This enables PyTorch users to collect GPU activity traces through the `rocprofiler-sdk` infrastructure and provides a stronger foundation for correctness, stability, and future profiling capabilities. The integration also positions PyTorch Profiler to benefit from additional `rocprofiler-sdk` capabilities as framework-level support continues to evolve.\\r\\n\\r\\n##### ROCprofiler-SDK beta support for Streaming Performance Monitors\\r\\n\\r\\n`rocprofiler-sdk` and `rocprofv3` add beta support for Streaming Performance Monitors (SPM), enabling selected hardware counters to be sampled over time while workloads execute. Unlike traditional counter collection, which captures a single aggregated value per kernel dispatch, SPM provides time-resolved hardware counter data. This is useful for analyzing long-running workloads and training jobs where temporal behavior matters as much as aggregate metrics. ROCpd support is planned for a future release.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn ROCm 7.14.0, SPM support is available through the `rocprofiler-sdk` API and `rocprofv3`. To enable SPM in `rocprofv3`, use the `--spm-beta-enabled` flag or set the `ROCPROFILER_SPM_BETA_ENABLED` environment variable. For API-based usage, set `ROCPROFILER_SPM_BETA_ENABLED`.\\r\\n\\r\\nSupported hardware: AMD Instinct MI300X, MI325X, MI350X, and MI355X GPUs.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor more information, see the [SPM API reference guide](https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/rocprofiler-sdk/en/latest/api-reference/spm.html) and the [SPM usage guide](https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/rocprofiler-sdk/en/latest/how-to/using-spm.html) for `rocprofv3`.\\r\\n\\r\\nSPM is a beta capability under active development and may affect system stability, including unexpected reboots. Do not use in production environments. See [ROCm known issues](#rocprofiler-spm-sessions-can-remain-in-a-stale-state-after-abrupt-termination) for current limitations.\\r\\n\\r\\n##### Selective ROCTx region profiling with counter collection\\r\\n\\r\\n`rocprofiler-sdk` and `rocprofv3` include support for profiling selected ROCTx regions, allowing users to focus profiling on specific application phases instead of collecting data for the entire workload. By inserting `roctxProfilerPause` and `roctxProfilerResume` markers in application code and using the `--selected-regions` option, only the GPU activity within the marked regions is captured. This helps reduce profiling noise and output size while making it easier to isolate performance behavior in targeted code paths. This is particularly useful for long-running workloads where full-execution traces are impractical.\\r\\n\\r\\nCounter collection for selected regions is available in ROCm 7.14.0. For details on `--selected-regions`, including usage with RCCL collectives and ROCTx markers, see [Using ROCprofiler-SDK ROCTx](https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/rocprofiler-sdk/en/latest/how-to/using-rocprofiler-sdk-roctx.html).\\r\\n\\r\\n##### Improved attach and re-attach profiling workflows\\r\\n\\r\\n`rocprofiler-sdk` and `rocprofv3` improve attach-based profiling workflows, allowing the profiler to connect to already-running GPU applications without requiring a restart. This supports production-style and long-running workloads where starting the application under the profiler is not always practical. Overall reliability and stability are also improved. Repeated attach and re-attach sessions now generate separate output files, making it easier to manage results from iterative profiling sessions. For details, see [Dynamic process attachment using rocprofv3](https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/rocprofiler-sdk/en/latest/how-to/using-rocprofv3-process-attachment.html).\\r\\n\\r\\n##### Reduced profiling overhead for counter collection\\r\\n\\r\\n`rocprofiler-sdk` reduces profiling overhead in ROCm 7.14.0, including customer-driven improvements for `rocprofv3` and SDK-based profiling paths. These changes make profiling more practical for performance-sensitive workflows and produce more representative trace data.\\r\\n\\r\\n##### ROCprof Trace Decoder decoupled from the ROCprofiler-SDK API\\r\\n\\r\\n`rocprof-trace-decoder` now has an independent public API, separate from the core `rocprofiler-sdk` API. The SQTT decoding API has moved into `rocprof-trace-decoder`; use the decoder's public API directly rather than `rocprofiler-sdk` for SQTT decoding. Previously, `rocprof-trace-decoder` was an internal plugin within `rocprofiler-sdk`, tightly coupling the two. The independent API can be versioned separately, allowing tools such as `rocpd` to consume the decoder without depending on the full SDK runtime. The `rocprofv3` end-user experience is unchanged.\\r\\n\\r\\n##### Quality and stability improvements\\r\\n\\r\\nThis release includes a range of quality and stability improvements across `rocprofiler-sdk` and `rocprofv3`. These include corrections to hardware counter reporting on specific GPU architectures, improvements to trace output accuracy, build fixes on newer GPU targets, expanded platform coverage in `aqlprofile`, and strengthened build and test support in TheRock CI. These changes improve the robustness and correctness of the profiling stack across supported hardware configurations.\\r\\n\\r\\n##### Queue interposition as a lighter alternative to queue interception\\r\\n\\r\\n`rocprofiler-sdk` introduces queue interposition, a mechanism that virtualizes HSA queue write-pointer operations without modifying the ROCR-Runtime or requiring full queue interception. For workloads that do not use dispatch counter collection, dispatch thread trace, or PC sampling, `rocprofiler-sdk` now defaults to this lighter interposition path, which reduces profiling overhead and improves overall stability. The legacy queue interception path remains in use when any of those features are active. The default behavior can be controlled via the `ROCPROFILER_QUEUE_INTERPOSITION` environment variable.\\r\\n\\r\\n##### ROCprof Compute Viewer 0.2.0 release\\r\\n\\r\\nROCprof Compute Viewer (RCV) 0.2.0 adds the ability to open raw `.att` and `.out` thread trace directories directly without a JSON conversion step, and introduces a Flamegraph view with per-CU and SIMD source and ISA stack rollups replacing the previous Explorer view. This release also adds hidden latency analysis for gfx10+ and Navi thread traces, SQTT instrumentation marker visualization, and a heuristic GPU Utilization derived counter, alongside fixes for scaling issues, Global View misalignments, and real-time alignment for both JSON and raw `.att` inputs. Installers are available for Windows (`.exe`) and macOS ARM64 (`.sh`), with GitHub Actions CI and release workflows now in place.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### ROCm Compute Profiler feature highlights\\r\\n\\r\\nThe following are notable enhancements to the ROCm Compute Profiler (rocprofiler-compute):\\r\\n\\r\\n* **PyTorch operator statistics (experimental)**: The PyTorch tracing (`--torch-trace`) now includes a per-operator statistics summary table, making it easier to spot hot operators and per-dispatch variance. The trace now also captures backward-pass and nested operators that were previously missed or misattributed.\\r\\n* **Faster analysis**: Analyze mode now processes profiling data more efficiently, reducing analysis time and memory usage on large workloads.\\r\\n\\r\\n* **Improved metric averaging accuracy**: Metric values across multiple kernel dispatches are now correctly weighted-averaged, eliminating errors that occurred when aggregating metrics with varying values across individual dispatches.\\r\\n\\r\\n* **pip installation support**: ROCm Compute Profiler is now available as a pip-installable Python package. A new `rocm-profiler` wheel on the ROCm Python package index lets you install ROCm Compute Profiler into a custom Python environment without building ROCm from source. The wheel package installs both ROCm Compute Profiler and ROCm Systems Profiler binaries. For installation instructions, see [Install ROCm Compute Profiler](https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/rocprofiler-compute/en/latest/install/core-install.html).\\r\\n\\r\\nFor more information, see the [ROCm Compute Profiler section](#rocm-compute-profiler-3-7-0) in the ROCm component changelogs.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### ROCm Systems Profiler feature highlights\\r\\n\\r\\nThe following are notable enhancements to ROCm Systems Profiler:\\r\\n\\r\\n* **GPU hardware counter sampling**: ROCm Systems Profiler now supports periodic sampling of Performance Metric Counters (PMCs). This lets you collect performance metrics at regular time intervals without serializing kernel dispatches, enabling profiling with significantly reduced overhead. For details, see the GPU metrics section in [Configuring runtime options](https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/rocprofiler-systems/en/latest/how-to/configuring-runtime-options.html).\\r\\n\\r\\n* **Unified memory profiling**: ROCm Systems Profiler now adds unified memory profiling with statistics on page migrations and page faults through a dedicated report section. This metric is opt-in and requires AMDGPU driver version 6.19.14 or later.\\r\\n\\r\\n* **Selective MPI rank profiling**: In MPI jobs, you can now restrict profile and trace output to a chosen subset of ranks, while unselected ranks run undisturbed. This cuts data volume and speeds up post-run analysis, and works across MPI implementations such as MPICH and Open MPI, including heterogeneous and multi-node environments. For details, see the rank filtering section in [Communication runtime profiling](https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/rocprofiler-systems/en/latest/how-to/communication-runtime-profiling.html).\\r\\n\\r\\n* **MPI rank console log control**: You can now limit console output to a specified subset of ranks while profiling and tracing continue on every rank. Existing behavior is preserved when no rank-selection option is set.\\r\\n\\r\\n* **Selective ROCTx region profiling**: When your application is instrumented with ROCTx region push and pop APIs, you can now include or exclude specific named regions to scope collection to the code paths you're investigating.\\r\\n\\r\\n* **pip installation support**: ROCm S"}

Summary\\r\\n\\r\\nThis PR started as a fix for AMD iGPU unified memory reporting on Strix Halo and grew into full AMD ROCm support for Windows plus targeted Linux fixes. 27 files changed, ~3,700 lines added.\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## 1. Strix Halo / AMD iGPU: unified memory detection (`hardware.py`, `amd.py`)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Problem:** `amd-smi` on iGPUs with unified/shared memory (e.g. Radeon 8060S / gfx1151 on Strix Halo) reports only the dedicated VRAM slice (~512 MB - 1 GB) rather than the full unified pool (~128 GB). `get_visible_gpu_utilization()` was returning `usable_gb ~= 0.35 GB`, producing a spurious \\\"Falling back to all visible GPUs -- model may not fit\\\" warning even with 100+ GB of unified memory available.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Fix:** Added `_reconcile_rocm_unified_memory()` and `_reconcile_primary_rocm_unified_memory()` (sharing a common `_apply_unified_memory_correction()` helper): after `amd-smi` returns a result on a ROCm device, cross-check each device's `vram_total_gb` against `torch.cuda.mem_get_info()`. When torch reports a larger total, replace the `amd-smi` VRAM fields in-place. No-op for discrete AMD GPUs where the two sources agree. Applied in both `get_gpu_utilization` and `get_visible_gpu_utilization`.\\r\\n\\r\\n> **Verified on Linux:** Radeon 8060S / gfx1151 / 128 GB unified ([@Chigoma333](https://github.com/Chigoma333), [@h34v3nzc0dex](https://github.com/h34v3nzc0dex))\\r\\n> **Windows Strix Halo:** code path implemented; hardware confirmation pending (Strix Halo devices do ship with Windows but no Windows Strix Halo tester has confirmed in this thread)\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## 2. Windows: AMD GPU detection (`install.ps1`, `setup.ps1`)\\r\\n\\r\\nBoth scripts now detect AMD GPUs on Windows with the same reliability as the Linux installer.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Full detection waterfall:** `hipinfo` (PATH) -> `hipinfo` (HIP_PATH\\\\bin / ROCM_PATH\\\\bin) -> `amd-smi list` -> `amd-smi static --asic` -> WMI marketing-name fallback. The AMD HIP SDK sets `HIP_PATH`/`ROCM_PATH` but does not always add the bin dir to `PATH`, so the env-var fallback handles this silently.\\r\\n- **Three-way message branching:**\\r\\n  - HIP SDK installed + GPU ROCm-accessible: normal ROCm install path\\r\\n  - HIP SDK installed + GPU not ROCm-accessible: `\\\"AMD GPU detected -- not ROCm-accessible (HIP 7.1.xxx)\\\"` with driver-issue explanation\\r\\n  - No HIP SDK: `\\\"AMD GPU detected -- HIP SDK not found\\\"` with install link\\r\\n- **Terminal visibility:** HIP SDK path and full `hipconfig --version` string shown as substeps under the `gpu` step on successful detection.\\r\\n- **Python 3.12 preference:** AMD ROCm users are steered toward Python 3.12 since AMD's index does not yet ship 3.13 wheels. GPU arch is detected before Python selection so the installer does not create a 3.13 venv that immediately needs to be recreated.\\r\\n- **gfx arch normalisation:** `gcnArchName` tokens are lowercased and feature suffixes stripped (e.g. `gfx1151:xnack-` -> `gfx1151`) before wheel-index lookup. `[regex]::Matches()` is used instead of `-match` to capture all GPU entries on multi-GPU hosts, and results are wrapped with `@()` to prevent PowerShell unwrapping a single-item result to a scalar string (which was previously causing the arch token to be indexed by character, returning `\\\"g\\\"` instead of `\\\"gfx1200\\\"`).\\r\\n- **`HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` / `ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES` respected** when selecting which GPU arch to install for on multi-GPU hosts.\\r\\n\\r\\n> **Verified on Windows:** RX 9060 XT / gfx1200 ([@LeoBorcherding](https://github.com/LeoBorcherding)), RX 7600 XT / gfx1102 ([@VELICAN-HACKS](https://github.com/VELICAN-HACKS))\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## 3. Windows: AMD ROCm PyTorch wheel installation (`install.ps1`, `install_python_stack.py`)\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Arch-aware wheel index:** Detected gfx arch maps to AMD's pip index at `https://repo.amd.com/rocm/whl/{arch_family}/`. Supported families: gfx1200/gfx1201 (RDNA 4), gfx1100/gfx1101/gfx1102/gfx1103 (RDNA 3), gfx1150/gfx1151 (Strix). `UNSLOTH_ROCM_WINDOWS_MIRROR` overrides the base URL for air-gapped installs.\\r\\n- **Newest release auto-selection:** Always picks the newest available ROCm release for the detected arch (e.g. rocm7.13 when available) rather than hardcoding a version.\\r\\n- **Full stack installed:** `torch`, `torchvision`, `torchaudio`, `rocm_sdk_core`, and `rocm_sdk_libraries_gfx*` installed together; wheel version cross-checking ensures the three torch packages are a matched set.\\r\\n- **ROCm torch repair:** Detects when dependency resolution (e.g. `torchao` or `unsloth`) overwrites the ROCm torch with a CPU wheel and reinstalls from the AMD index.\\r\\n- **`HIP_PATH` fallback in Python stack:** `_detect_windows_gfx_arch()` probes `HIP_PATH\\\\bin` / `ROCM_PATH\\\\bin` when `hipinfo` is not on `PATH`, then falls back to `amd-smi` as a third tier, so `_ensure_rocm_torch()` does not silently skip ROCm wheels on runtime-only AMD installs.\\r\\n- **`rocm7.2` index enabled:** Previously commented out of `_ROCM_TORCH_INDEX` pending a torch upper bound bump. Now enabled with a matching `_ROCM_TORCH_PKG_SPECS` entry (`torch>=2.11.0,<2.12.0`).\\r\\n\\r\\n> **Verified on Windows:** RX 9060 XT / gfx1200, torch==2.11.0+rocm7.13.0 from repo.amd.com ([@LeoBorcherding](https://github.com/LeoBorcherding)); RX 7600 XT / gfx1102, torch==2.9.0+rocmsdk ([@VELICAN-HACKS](https://github.com/VELICAN-HACKS))\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## 4. Windows: ROCm runtime patches (`worker.py`, `main.py`, `hardware.py`)\\r\\n\\r\\nSeveral issues in AMD's current Windows wheel require workarounds at startup. All patches are scoped to Windows ROCm only (gated on active HIP runtime via `torch.version.hip` or `'rocm' in torch.__version__`) and self-retire when AMD ships fixes.\\r\\n\\r\\n### `torch._C._distributed_c10d` missing\\r\\n`torch._C` is a compiled C extension on Windows ROCm. Python cannot do submodule imports from it, so `torch._C._distributed_c10d` does not exist, causing import failures when `torch.distributed` is loaded. A populated `sys.modules` stub is injected before `import torch.distributed`, exposing `FakeProcessGroup`, `ProcessGroup`, `Work`, `Store`, and all other symbols. The `if name not in sys.modules` guard means this self-retires the moment AMD fixes their build (tracked: [ROCm/TheRock#3284](https://github.com/ROCm/TheRock/issues/3284)).\\r\\n\\r\\n### `torchao` stubs\\r\\n`torchao` imports `torch.distributed._functional_collectives` at module level, which crashes on Windows ROCm via the missing C backend. `torchao` is stubbed with a custom `_StubTypeMeta` metaclass so `isinstance(x, StubClass)` returns `False` (not `TypeError`) since peft's LoRA torchao path calls `isinstance()` on the imported types. A `_StubSubpackageFinder` meta path finder auto-stubs any depth of `torchao.xxx.yyy` imports. Scoped to Windows ROCm only so real torchao is unaffected on Windows NVIDIA.\\r\\n\\r\\n### `BNB_ROCM_VERSION` in server process\\r\\nThe server process (`main.py`) and training worker are separate processes, so env vars set in the worker are not visible to the server. `main.py` now scans `libbitsandbytes_rocm*.dll` at startup to detect the installed DLL suffix and sets `BNB_ROCM_VERSION` before any bitsandbytes import, eliminating the `\\\"Configured ROCm binary not found\\\"` error. DLL directory handles are retained at module scope in `_ROCM_DLL_HANDLES` in both `main.py` and `worker.py` so they are not garbage-collected. Falls back to `\\\"72\\\"` when no DLL is found.\\r\\n\\r\\n### `_grouped_mm` null kernel (gfx1200, ROCm <= 7.12)\\r\\nOn Windows ROCm with HIP < 7.13, `torch._grouped_mm` dispatches to a null HIP kernel on gfx1200, causing a `0xC0000005` access violation (crash) during training. A Python fallback implementation is patched in via `torch.library.Library` on the CUDA dispatch key when `HIP < 7.13`. The fallback handles 2-D (`mm`), 3-D batched (`bmm`/`matmul`), and grouped-with-offsets inputs. Bypassed entirely on HIP >= 7.13 where AMD fixed the kernel. The `torch.library.Library` registration is kept at module scope in `_WINDOWS_ROCM_GROUPED_MM_LIB` to prevent garbage collection mid-run.\\r\\n\\r\\n### `amd-smi` circuit breaker\\r\\n`amd-smi` on some Windows installs returns non-zero or opens console popups. GPU polling disables itself after 3 consecutive failures (`_AMD_SMI_FAILURE_LIMIT = 3`) and all `amd-smi` subprocess calls suppress console windows via `windows_hidden_subprocess_kwargs()`. The default timeout is also raised from 5s to 30s on Windows (10s on Linux) to accommodate the cold-hardware ROCm runtime initialisation cost.\\r\\n\\r\\n### `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` support\\r\\n`HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` is now honoured in `_get_parent_visible_gpu_spec` and `apply_gpu_ids` sets `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` for ROCm training workers, parallel to `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` on NVIDIA.\\r\\n\\r\\n> **Verified on Windows:** full QLoRA training run on unsloth/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct / unsloth/alpaca-cleaned completed successfully on RX 9060 XT / gfx1200 / ROCm 7.13 ([@LeoBorcherding](https://github.com/LeoBorcherding))\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## 5. Windows: ROCm inference fix (`llama_cpp.py`)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Problem:** The llama.cpp prebuilt bundles its own `rocblas.dll` next to the binary but not the Tensile kernel library files it depends on at runtime (`rocblas/library/TensileLibrary*.dat` + `.hsaco`). When rocBLAS initialises for the first real GEMM (prefill), it searches for those files relative to its own location which does not exist in the prebuilt install tree, causing a crash with `WinError 10054`/`10061`. This is why the crash only appeared on the first generation request and not during model load.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Fix:** Set `ROCBLAS_TENSILE_LIBPATH` in the llama-server subprocess env to `<HIP_PATH>\\\\bin\\\\rocblas\\\\library` when the directory exists. Uses `setdefault` so a user-supplied value is never overwritten. No-op on CUDA/CPU and Linux.\\r\\n\\r\\n> **Verified on Windows:** gfx1200 / RX 9060 XT ([@LeoBorcherding](https://github.com/LeoBorcherding)), gfx1102 / RX 7600 XT, inference no longer falling back to CPU after fix ([@VELICAN-HACKS](https://github.com/VELICAN-HACKS))\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## 6. Windows: `install_llama_prebuilt.py`\\r\\n\\r\\n- `_resolve_exe()` added: checks PATH then `HIP_PATH\\\\bin` / `ROCM_PATH\\\\bin` before giving up, so `has_rocm` is not silently `False` on machines where the HIP SDK bin dir is not on PATH.\\r\\n- HIP asset (`llama-{tag}-bin-win-hip-radeon-x64.zip`) added to the simple-policy Windows path so the HIP prebuilt is selected when ROCm is detected.\\r\\n- `--has-rocm` flag added: `setup.ps1` passes its own detection result through so the prebuilt installer does not need to re-run `hipinfo`/`amd-smi` internally.\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## 7. Linux: Strix Halo + ROCm 7.1 routing fix (`install.sh`, `install_python_stack.py`)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Problem:** ROCm 7.1 has a driver bug causing a segfault in `torch._grouped_mm` (`moe_utils.py:167`) on gfx1151/gfx1150. The Radeon repo began shipping Python 3.13 wheels for `rocm-rel-7.1`, so the installer was silently landing on the broken combo even for users who expected rocm7.2.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Fix:** When gfx1151 or gfx1150 is detected and `TORCH_INDEX_URL` is `*/rocm7.1`, the installer overrides to `https://repo.amd.com/rocm/whl/gfx1151/` (AMD's arch-specific index), landing users on `torch==2.11.0+rocm7.13.0` which has the actual `_grouped_mm` kernel fix. `UNSLOTH_AMD_ROCM_MIRROR` overrides the base URL for air-gapped installs. `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES`/`ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES` are respected on mixed iGPU+dGPU setups so the override only fires when the runtime-target GPU is actually a Strix arch. Also: ROCm tag normalisation now uses explicit `case` arms (e.g. `rocm7.1|rocm7.1.*`) so a future `rocm7.10` does not match `rocm7.1*`. `install.sh` also adds a sysfs KFD topology fallback (`/sys/class/kfd/kfd/topology/nodes/*/properties`) for AMD detection when neither `rocminfo` nor `amd-smi` is available, and explicit warning messages when ROCm version cannot be determined.\\r\\n\\r\\n> **Verified on Linux:** gfx1151 / Radeon 8060S / Ubuntu 24.04 / ROCm 7.13 nightly: `_check_torch_grouped_mm_supported() == True`, no segfault, `pip download` resolves `torch==2.11.0+rocm7.13.0` from the AMD index ([@h34v3nzc0dex](https://github.com/h34v3nzc0dex)); gfx1201 / Radeon AI PRO R9700 / CachyOS ([@jgreenburg](https://github.com/jgreenburg))\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## 8. Linux: Ubuntu 24.04 + ROCm 7.x llama.cpp build fix (`setup.sh`)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Problem:** ROCm 7.x ships clang-20, which on Ubuntu 24.04 selects `/usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/14` (a runtime-only dir with no C++ headers) as its default GCC install dir, causing `fatal error: 'cstdlib' file not found` during the llama.cpp HIP source build.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Fix:** `setup.sh` uses `gcc -print-multiarch` to determine the correct multiarch path (falling back to `$(uname -m)-linux-gnu`), then iterates gcc 14->11 to find the first version with both a runtime dir and `/usr/include/c++/<ver>` headers, and passes `--gcc-install-dir=<path>` via `CMAKE_HIP_FLAGS`.\\r\\n\\r\\n> **Verified on Linux:** picks `/usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/13` on Ubuntu 24.04; clean 417/417 llama.cpp build for gfx1151 ([@h34v3nzc0dex](https://github.com/h34v3nzc0dex))\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## 9. GPU OOM guard (`worker.py`)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Problem:** On ROCm GPUs (confirmed on RDNA 4 gfx1200/gfx1201 and Strix Halo gfx1151), exhausting VRAM/unified memory can cause the HIP driver to hang the GPU ring buffer rather than raising a Python `OutOfMemoryError`, resulting in a full system freeze requiring a hard reboot.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Fix:** `torch.cuda.set_per_process_memory_fraction()` is called at worker startup on ROCm only:\\r\\n- **Discrete cards:** `0.90` -- leaves ~1.6 GB headroom on a 16 GB card for HIP context and allocator fragmentation.\\r\\n- **Unified-memory APUs (gfx1150/gfx1151):** `0.80` -- the unified pool is shared with the host OS and page cache. 0.90 x 128 GB would leave only ~13 GB for the entire system, reproducing the freeze rather than preventing it.\\r\\n\\r\\nClassification uses `gcnArchName` stripped of feature suffixes (e.g. `gfx1151:xnack-` -> `gfx1151`), checked against `{\\\"gfx1150\\\", \\\"gfx1151\\\"}`. This is naming-independent and avoids the marketing-name ambiguity between Strix Point (`890M`) and Strix Halo (`8060S`). The OOM exception handler also surfaces a clear, actionable UI message with concrete remediation steps instead of a raw HIP error string.\\r\\n\\r\\n> **Verified on Windows:** gfx1200 / RX 9060 XT: training session that previously froze the machine now terminates cleanly with an OOM error ([@LeoBorcherding](https://github.com/LeoBorcherding))\\r\\n> **Verified on Linux:** gfx1151 / Radeon 8060S / 128 GB unified: `set_per_process_memory_fraction(0.80)` accepted, `_is_unified=True`, 102.4 GiB cap, 25.6 GiB left for OS ([@h34v3nzc0dex](https://github.com/h34v3nzc0dex))\\r\\n> **Windows Strix Halo:** gcnArchName classification will apply the 0.80 fraction; hardware confirmation pending\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## 10. Tests (`tests/studio/install/test_rocm_support.py`)\\r\\n\\r\\n~1,231 lines of new test coverage:\\r\\n- `TestStrixHaloGfxArchDetection` -- arch detection waterfall (hipinfo PATH / HIP_PATH / amd-smi)\\r\\n- `TestHipSdkEnvPathResolution` -- `HIP_PATH`/`ROCM_PATH` fallback for `hipinfo`/`hipconfig`\\r\\n- `TestHipSdkDetectedSubstep` -- terminal output substeps on AMD detection\\r\\n- `TestStrixRocm71Override` -- Strix routing to AMD arch-specific index;
